chapters.title: An outright is three opinions in a trench coat
chapters.dek: Buy a call and you have bet on direction, on volatility and on time. You probably only meant one of them.

figures.title: The same directional view, with and without the second leg
figures.caption: The upper panel is what you gain and give up in the payoff. The lower one is what you gain and give up in exposure — and it is the panel people skip. Drag the volatility shift and watch the outright swing while the spread barely moves.

checks.q: You are bullish and buy a call. The stock does nothing for a week and you lose 12%. What happened?
checks.right: Some of it is theta, and probably most of it is vega. An outright call is long volatility as well as long direction, and you only expressed one of those views
checks.why: Theta and vega, and it is usually the vega that surprises people. A five-point volatility drop costs 25.2% on this outright and a week of theta costs a fraction of that. The whole reason to spread is that you can keep the view you have and stop paying for the ones you do not.

chapters.text: Suppose you think a 100 stock is going to 110 over the next three months. The obvious trade is to buy a call. The obvious trade also commits you to two other views you never expressed. Buy the 105 call at 3.9341 . You are now long 0.194 of vega per point — so if implied volatility drops five points overnight with the stock unchanged, the option is worth 2.9419 and you have lost 25.2% of your money having been exactly right about nothing happening yet. Now sell the 115 call against it. The package costs 2.5151 and carries 0.0568 of vega — 71% less . The same five-point volatility drop costs 13.9% instead of 25.2%. You have kept most of the directional exposure and thrown away most of the exposure you did not want. That is the entire argument for spreading, and it generalizes. Every additional leg is an opportunity to cancel a sensitivity you are not being paid to hold. A calendar cancels direction and keeps term structure. A butterfly cancels direction and most of the vega and keeps the distribution's shape. A risk reversal cancels most of the volatility level and keeps skew. Two things you give up, and they are real. The spread caps the upside — above 115 the short call gives back everything the long call earns. And it doubles the transaction costs, which page 14 prices: two spreads crossed instead of one, on options whose spreads are wide in volatility terms. So spreading is not free and it is not automatically better. It is a way of paying, in upside and in commission, to stop being exposed to things you have no view on. Whether that is worth it is the subject of the rest of the page. chapters.title: The vertical, and the credit-spread illusion
chapters.dek: A bull call spread and a bull put spread on the same strikes are the same trade. The difference is eleven cents of interest.

figures.title: Call spread and put spread, drawn on top of each other
figures.caption: The lower panel is the claim: the difference between a "debit spread" and a "credit spread" is a horizontal line, not a shape. Widen the strikes, move the expiry, change the rate — the line moves up and down and stays flat, because it is interest on the width and nothing else.

checks.q: A trader says they prefer selling credit spreads because "you collect premium and time decay works for you". What is wrong?
checks.right: The equivalent debit spread has identical payoff, maximum profit, maximum loss and breakeven. Both are the same position, so both have the same theta. Collecting cash up front is a financing difference of about eleven cents
checks.why: They are describing the same position twice. The bull put spread and the bull call spread on the same strikes are one trade — if one has favorable decay so does the other, because they are identical. What genuinely differs is margin treatment, assignment risk on the short leg ( page 04 ) and the eleven cents of interest. Those are worth choosing on; the payoff diagram is not.

terms.Vertical spread: Two options of the same type and expiry at different strikes. The basic directional spread, and the one whose credit and debit versions are the same trade.

chapters.text: The vertical is the basic directional spread: two options, same type, same expiry, different strikes. Buy the 100 call and sell the 110 call and you have paid 3.6607 for a position that can make at most 6.3393 , loses at most what you paid, and breaks even at 103.6607 . Now do it the other way. Sell the 100 put and buy the 110 put — a "credit spread" — and you receive 6.2290 . Different options, different cash flow, and a whole vocabulary of trading advice built on the distinction. It is the same trade. Line the two P&L profiles up across every terminal price and they differ by a constant 0.110346 at every single point — at 80, at 95, at 110, at 120, identically. That constant is not a strategic difference. It is interest: the width of the spread is 10, the debit plus the credit is 9.889654 , and the gap is exactly 10 × (1 − e^−rT) — the financing on the width over ninety days, which the credit version collects because the cash arrives today. So "I prefer credit spreads because I collect premium" is a statement about cash flow and margin treatment, not about risk. The two positions have the same payoff diagram, the same maximum profit, the same maximum loss and the same breakeven. Choosing between them is a financing and operational decision — which is a real decision, and a completely different one from the one people think they are making. The other trap in this chapter is reward-to-risk . The 100/110 spread offers 1.73 to 1; the 100/105 offers 1.33 to 1. That ranking says nothing about which is better, because it says nothing about how likely each outcome is. A structure with a 20:1 reward-to-risk that needs a 30% move is not generous; it is a lottery ticket with the odds printed on the other side. [equation: debit + credit = (K_2 − K_1) · e^−rT] Reads as: what you pay for the call spread plus what you receive for the put spread is the width of the spread, discounted. That identity is why the two are the same position — it is put–call parity applied to both legs. chapters.title: Five ways to be bullish, and none of them wins
chapters.dek: Identical starting delta. Five structures lead in five different regions, and the lead changes hands four times.

figures.title: Five bullish structures at identical delta
figures.caption: The strip below the chart is the answer to "which is best" — and it has five bands. Drag the strikes and the bands move, but they never collapse into one. There is no structure that wins everywhere, which is the honest version of every "best options strategy" article ever written.

figures.title: Live with your choice
figures.caption: In the first future the stock finishes at $130.52: the long call makes $5,128 and the 1×2 ratio loses $23,637. Over 200 futures in which the view is right, the short put is the best structure 34% of the time, the ratio 28% and the long call 24%, and stock and the call spread never come first. Yet the ratio, best in more than a quarter of futures, averages a loss of $992, because the big rallies run straight through its short strikes; the long call averages the most, $308. Being right about direction does not choose the structure for you.

checks.q: All five structures start with 100 deltas. What does that tell you about their risk?
checks.right: Almost nothing. Delta matches them only for the first small move — their gamma runs from +669 to −4,160 and their vega from +46 to −287, so they diverge immediately and violently
checks.why: Almost nothing. Matching delta matches the first derivative at one point — which is exactly page 23's lesson about how fast a local approximation stops describing a position. These five agree on the first penny of movement and disagree by tens of thousands of dollars on the outcome.

terms.Ratio spread: More options sold than bought. The payoff peaks and then turns over, so the worst case arrives precisely when your directional view was most right.

chapters.text: Here is the comparison the textbooks describe and rarely draw. You are bullish on a 100 stock over ninety days. Five option structures express that — with the stock itself drawn as a baseline — and to compare them honestly each is sized so they all start with exactly 100 share-deltas — identical directional exposure, so the only differences are structural. The sizes are already revealing. A hundred deltas costs $10,000 as stock, $936 as long 105 calls, $1,122 as a 105/115 call spread, and −$954 as short 95 puts — you are paid to take the position. The 1×2 call ratio needs a size of 35.6 spreads to reach a hundred deltas, because each one starts with almost none. Then the outcomes, and this is the point of the page. If the stock falls to 80 , the long call is the best of the lot, losing $936 — its whole cost — while the short put loses $4,011 . At 95 to 105 , where nothing much happens, the short put is best at +$954 and the long call is the worst, losing its entire premium. Just below that, at 90 , the risk reversal — long the 115 call, short the 90 put, put on for a small credit — is the only line in profit at all, by $14 . At 110 to 120 the ratio spread dominates everything, making $31,734 at 115. And at 130 the ratio has collapsed to a $21,727 loss while the plain long call — worst-in-class over most of the range — is the best of them all at +$5,014 . Five structures, one view, identical initial delta, and the lead changes hands four times across five distinct regions. The long call is simultaneously the best trade if you are wrong, the worst trade if you are slightly right, and the best trade again if you are extremely right. Which means "what is the best bullish structure" is not a question with an answer. The question with an answer is how right do you expect to be, and how wrong can you afford to be — and each of these five encodes a different reply. The chart above is every outcome at once. Trading is one outcome at a time. Pick a structure, then play futures: in every one of them the stock really does drift up 15% a year, so your bullish view is right. Live with your choice Your structure In the first future the stock finishes at $130.52: the long call makes $5,128 and the 1×2 ratio loses $23,637. Over 200 futures in which the view is right, the short put is the best structure 34% of the time, the ratio 28% and the long call 24%, and stock and the call spread never come first. Yet the ratio, best in more than a quarter of futures, averages a loss of $992, because the big rallies run straight through its short strikes; the long call averages the most, $308. Being right about direction does not choose the structure for you. Trader's lens Traders pick structures from a distribution, not a target. "Bullish" is not a view until it says how far, how fast, and how wrong you can afford to be. The structure that is most often best is rarely the one with the best average, and the one with the best average is rarely the one that survives the worst future. Short premium wins often and small; long premium wins rarely and big. Check which one your account can sit through. A structure that is best in the most futures can still be the worst trade, if its bad futures are bad enough. Size every alternative to the same delta before comparing them, or the comparison is just leverage. Rule of thumb: write down the move you expect and the move that would hurt, then pick the structure that wins the first and survives the second.

chapters.title: What you actually signed up for
chapters.dek: Same delta, opposite everything else. The greek table is the contract you did not read.

figures.title: The same hundred deltas, five different contracts
figures.caption: Read the bars as "how much of something else am I buying per unit of the thing I wanted". The ratio spread's bars leave the chart, which is the visual version of the sentence: it is not a directional trade.

checks.q: Two structures both have 100 deltas. One has +669 of gamma cash and one has −4,160. What are you really choosing between?
checks.right: A long-volatility trade and a short-volatility trade that happen to share a directional tilt. The volatility exposure is the larger part of both
checks.why: You are choosing a volatility view. The shared delta is the smallest thing these two have in common. This is the same trap page 09 describes from the other end: a structure has a payoff description and an exposure description, and the exposure description is the one that determines what happens to you between now and expiry.

chapters.text: Chapter 03 showed the outcomes. This is the mechanism, and it fits in one table. Every structure carries the same hundred deltas and completely different second-order exposure. The long 105 call runs gamma-cash of +669 , vega of +46.20 and theta of −8.30 a day. You are long movement, long volatility, and paying rent for both. The short 95 put runs gamma-cash of −830 , vega of −57.33 and theta of +7.57 . Same direction, opposite everything else: you are short movement, short volatility, and collecting rent. The 105/115 call spread is the moderate version — +367 of gamma, +25.33 of vega, −5.04 of theta — roughly half the long call's second-order exposure for the same first-order exposure, which is chapter 01's argument in numbers. The 1×2 call ratio is in a different category: −4,160 of gamma-cash and −287 of vega on a position that is nominally just "bullish". That is five times the short put's gamma and five times its vega. The ratio is a short-volatility trade wearing a directional label, which is why chapter 03 showed it making $31,734 in one place and losing $21,727 in another. So the greek table is where the disguise comes off. Two structures with the same delta and opposite gamma are not two versions of the same view — they are a directional view bundled with a volatility view, and the second one is frequently larger. The practical habit that follows: before putting on any spread, look at its gamma, vega and theta per unit of delta. If those numbers are large relative to the delta you wanted, the trade is mostly not about direction, whatever you called it when you decided to do it. chapters.title: Ratios: the spread that turns on you
chapters.dek: Sell more than you buy and the payoff has a peak. Past that peak it goes down forever.

figures.title: Ratio and backspread, with their breakevens
figures.caption: The tent and the valley are mirror images and both are drawn from the same two strikes. Watch the upper breakeven in the lower panel as you raise the ratio — the move from 1×2 to 1×3 brings the point of no return in dramatically, which is why the extra premium is not free.

checks.q: Your 1×2 call ratio is at its maximum profit. The stock keeps rallying. What happens?
checks.right: You give it all back and then lose without limit. Past 123.90 the position is a naked short call, and the loss grows one-for-one with the stock
checks.why: It becomes a naked short call. The peak is not a cap, it is a turning point — which is the single most important thing to know about ratios and the thing their payoff diagram makes look benign. Being spectacularly right about direction is the scenario that hurts, and no other structure on this page has that property.

terms.Backspread: More bought than sold — the mirror of a ratio. Limited risk, and it needs a large move to pay.

chapters.text: A ratio spread buys one option and sells more than one further out. Our 1×2 — long one 105 call, short two 115 calls — is a net debit of 1.0961 , and its payoff is a tent: nothing much below 105, rising to a peak of 8.904 at 115, then falling away. The number that matters is where it crosses back through zero on the way down: 123.904 . Above that the position loses money, and it keeps losing without limit, because you are net short one call. That single fact makes the ratio a fundamentally different animal from everything else on this page. A vertical's worst case is its debit. A ratio's worst case is unbounded and is realized precisely when your directional view was most right. It is the only structure here that punishes you for being too correct. Turn it around and you get a backspread : sell one near option, buy two further out. Now the payoff is a valley — you lose in the middle and win big at the edges, with limited risk. Backspreads are long volatility with a directional tilt; ratios are short volatility with a directional tilt. The reason ratios get traded despite the tail is that the tent covers the region where the stock usually ends up, and the premium collected pays for the middle. That is a real edge and it is also the exact shape of a strategy that works repeatedly and then removes a year of profit in a week. Page 08's earnings-straddle chapter is the same distributional shape seen from the other side: high win rate, negative tail, and a mean that hides both. The figure lets you drag the ratio and the strikes so you can watch the upper breakeven move. Two things to notice: widening the gap between strikes raises the peak and moves the breakeven further away, and raising the ratio from 1×2 to 1×3 does the opposite in a hurry. chapters.title: The same view, capped and uncapped
chapters.dek: A short straddle and a long butterfly both want the stock to sit still. One of them can end your year.

figures.title: Short straddle against long butterfly
figures.caption: The two payoff curves cross twice and the region between them is what the cap costs. The lower panel is the part the payoff diagram hides: under a volatility shock the straddle's mark moves several times as far, because the butterfly's wings are long the same volatility its body is short.

checks.q: Implied volatility jumps eight points overnight with the stock unchanged. You are short a straddle and your colleague is long a butterfly on the same strikes. Who is hurt more?
checks.right: The straddle, by a wide margin. It is short vega across the whole surface, while the butterfly's long wings offset most of what its short body loses
checks.why: The straddle, and it is not close. Both positions want the stock to sit still, and only one of them is meaningfully short vega. That is why a butterfly is often described as a "cheap" way to be short volatility — the description is right about the cash and wrong about the reason, which is that most of the vega has been hedged away by the wings rather than discounted.

chapters.text: Suppose the view is not directional at all: you think the stock stays near 100 and implied volatility is too high. Two structures express it, and comparing them is the cleanest illustration of what capping risk actually costs. Short the 100 straddle. You receive 11.0586 . If the stock finishes at 100 you keep all of it. If it finishes at 85 or 115 you lose 3.941 . If it finishes at 130 you lose about nineteen, and there is no bound on that number. Buy the 90/100/110 butterfly. You pay 2.7243 . If the stock finishes at 100 you make 7.276 . If it finishes at 85 or 115 you lose 2.7243 — your entire cost — and that is the worst that can ever happen, at any price, forever. So the butterfly gives up about a third of the best case and removes the entire tail. The trade-off is priced, as it should be, and the question of which to prefer is a question about how you size rather than about which is "better". The subtle part is what the two positions are made of. Both are short volatility, but the straddle is short volatility everywhere while the butterfly is short volatility only near the body and long the wings. So a move to 130 that would be catastrophic for the straddle is merely the butterfly's ordinary maximum loss — and a large rise in implied volatility hurts the straddle much more, because the butterfly's long wings absorb most of it. Which points at the practical rule. Structures that look similar in payoff can behave very differently in vega , and structures with the same vega can behave very differently in the tail. Reading either dimension alone gets you a surprise eventually. chapters.title: Choosing, and the question that actually decides it
chapters.dek: Not "am I right" but "how right, how soon, and how wrong can I afford to be".

figures.title: Best structure by outcome and volatility change
figures.caption: Each cell is colored by whichever of the five structures makes the most money in that scenario. The map is not a recommendation — it is a demonstration that the recommendation depends entirely on a cell you cannot know in advance, which is why the four questions above are the actual method.

checks.q: You are mildly bullish, have no volatility view, and cannot tolerate a large loss. Which of the five fits best?
checks.right: The call spread. It keeps the direction, carries about half the long call's vega, and its maximum loss is the debit — the only one of the five that matches all three constraints
checks.why: The call spread. Work the constraints: no volatility view rules out the long call and the short put, both of which carry large vega; intolerance of a large loss rules out the short put and the ratio, whose worst cases are many times the premium. The ratio does profit most from a mild rise — and its unbounded tail fails the third constraint, which is exactly the trade-off chapter 05 is about.

chapters.text: Everything above assembles into a decision, and the decision is not made on the payoff diagram. Chapter 03 established that no structure dominates. What remains is to be explicit about the four questions whose answers pick one. How right do you expect to be? A modest move favors spreads and short-premium structures; a large move favors outright long options, which is why the long call was the worst structure over most of chapter 03's range and the best at 130. Capping the upside is only cheap if you did not need it. How wrong can you afford to be? The long call's maximum loss is its premium. The short put's is many times that. The ratio's is unbounded. These are not refinements of one another; they are different businesses, and position sizing has to be done on the worst case rather than on the delta. What is your volatility view? Chapter 04 showed that structures matched on delta run gamma from +669 to −4,160. If you have no volatility view, the honest choice is the structure with the least of it — and that is usually a spread rather than an outright. When do you need to be right? Theta runs from −8.30 a day to +7.57 across the same five structures. A long option needs the move to arrive before the premium decays; a short-premium structure needs the move not to arrive, and is happy to wait. The figure puts those together as a scenario grid — outcome across, volatility change down, best structure in each cell. It is the same instrument as page 23's scenario matrix, applied to a choice rather than to a book, and it has the same lesson: the answer lives in the corners, and no single number on the entry ticket predicts it. The honest summary of this page is that "which spread should I use" is underdetermined until you have said something about magnitude, timing, volatility and tolerance. Most bad structure choices are not errors of arithmetic. They are answers to a question that was never fully asked. chapters.title: Drill it, then check yourself
chapters.dek: Breakevens, maximum losses and reward-to-risk, at the speed you need them on a screen.

figures.caption: Core covers vertical breakevens and maximum profit and loss; Full adds ratio turning points and the credit–debit identity.

checks.q: Why sell a further-out call against a call you have bought?
checks.right: To cancel exposures you did not intend. The spread carries 71% less vega than the outright, so a five-point volatility drop costs 13.9% instead of 25.2%
checks.why: To stop paying for views you do not have. The cost is the capped upside and a second bid-offer to cross. Whether that is worth it depends on how large a move you expect, which is chapter 07's first question.

checks.q: A 100/110 bull call spread costs 3.66. What does the 100/110 bull put spread pay?
checks.right: About 6.23 — the two must sum to the width discounted, 10 × e^(−rT) = 9.89
checks.why: 6.23. The identity is put–call parity applied to both strikes, so the debit and credit always sum to the discounted width. That is why the two positions are the same trade, differing by eleven cents of interest.

checks.q: Five bullish structures at identical delta. How many times does the lead change hands across outcomes from 80 to 130?
checks.right: Four times, across five regions. The long call leads at 80, the risk reversal at 90, the short put from 95 to 105, the ratio from 110 to 120, and the long call again at 130
checks.why: Four changes, five regions. The long call is simultaneously the best structure if you are wrong, the worst if you are slightly right, and the best again if you are extremely right. There is no dominant choice, which is the whole page.

checks.q: A 1×2 call ratio sized to 100 deltas carries −4,160 of gamma cash. What is it really?
checks.right: A short-volatility position with a directional tilt. Its gamma is five times the short put's and its vega is −287 against the long call's +46
checks.why: A short-volatility trade wearing a directional label. Which is exactly why it made $31,734 in one cell of chapter 03 and lost $21,727 in another — outcomes that have nothing to do with the hundred deltas it started with.

checks.q: Your 1×2 ratio peaks at 8.90 and you paid 1.10. Where does it stop making money?
checks.right: At 123.90. Above that it is a naked short call and the loss grows without limit
checks.why: 123.90 — the peak plus what you paid, measured from the short strike. The peak is a turning point, not a cap, and the scenario that produces the unbounded loss is the one where your directional view was most correct.

checks.q: A short straddle receives 11.06 and a long butterfly on the same body costs 2.72. What does the butterfly buy you?
checks.right: A bounded worst case. Its maximum loss is 2.72 at any price forever, against an unbounded loss for the straddle — paid for by giving up about a third of the best case
checks.why: A bounded worst case. Both positions want the stock to sit still; only one of them can remove a year of profit in a week. The butterfly also carries far less vega, because its long wings offset the short body — which is the part the payoff diagram does not show.
